lead: Solid-state welding joins two metals without melting either. Clean faces are pressed together and heated below the melting point; atoms cross the interface and the pieces become one. No molten pool means no cast nugget, no gas porosity and no hot cracking. The process suits aluminium alloys that arc welding handles badly, and pairs of different metals that form brittle compounds when molten. Friction stir welded panels ride in trains and ships; friction welded shafts sit in cars and drilling rigs.
prereq: You need the three-way classification of chapter 4.1, and plastic deformation and recrystallisation from Unit 2, Bulk Metal Forming Processes.

blocks.text: Every solid-state process needs three things. Surfaces must be clean, because oxide and grease hold atoms apart. They must be forced into intimate contact, with pressure high enough to flatten surface asperities. Heat and time must then let atoms diffuse across the original interface.
Temperature stays below the melting point, usually 0.5 to 0.9 of the melting point on the absolute scale, in kelvin.

blocks.where: T<sub>join</sub> is interface temperature in kelvin; T<sub>m</sub> is melting point of the parent metal in kelvin.

blocks.text: Fusion welding melts metal and freezes it as a cast nugget in a heat-affected zone. That nugget is coarser and weaker than wrought parent metal, and melting brings porosity, hot cracking and loss of alloying elements. Solid-state joining skips the melt: wrought structure survives and the heat-affected zone stays narrow. It also joins metals that form brittle intermetallic compounds when molten, such as aluminium to steel.

The cost is hardware. Parts must be clean and closely fitted, and the machine needs heavy clamps plus a press, spindle or vibration source. These processes finish the classification of chapter 4.1: the parent metal stays solid from start to end.
Rotary friction welding holds one part in a spinning chuck and the other in a stationary clamp, then pushes them together with axial force.

items: Contact: faces rub at v = πDN/60 and friction makes heat.
Friction heating: in seconds the interface reaches 0.8 to 0.9 T<sub>m</sub>. Metal softens but no pool forms.
Burn-off: axial force squeezes softened, oxide-covered metal out as flash. A fixed burn-off length passes.
Braking: drive stops and rotation ends.
Upset: a larger axial force forges the hot faces together. Flash is machined off later.

blocks.text: Controlling variables are rotational speed, friction pressure, burn-off length, upset pressure and upset time. A cycle takes seconds and runs without an operator.

Linear friction welding replaces spin with back-and-forth oscillation of a few millimetres at about 50 Hz under pressure. It joins flat, non-round parts, such as compressor blades to a disk to make a blisk.
Uses: axle and drive shafts, drill pipes, valve bodies, tool shanks, aluminium-to-steel transition joints.

blocks.where: v is rubbing speed at the interface in m/s; D is diameter of the rotating part in m; N is rotational speed in rev/min.

blocks.text: Friction stir welding (FSW) uses a non-consumable rotating tool with a shoulder, a flat disc that rubs the top surface, and a pin (probe), a short stub that projects into the joint line.

items: Plunge: the spinning tool is pushed into the joint until the shoulder touches the plate.
Dwell: a few seconds of rubbing raise the metal to about 0.8 T<sub>m</sub>.
Traverse: the tool moves along the joint. Softened metal flows around the pin and the shoulder forges it behind the tool.
Withdraw: the tool lifts out and leaves an exit hole, later cut off or filled.

blocks.text: No melting happens. The pin leaves a stir zone of fine, recrystallised grains, flanked by a thermomechanically affected zone and an ordinary heat-affected zone.
Aluminium alloys of the 2xxx, 6xxx and 7xxx families hot crack, porosify or lose strength in arc welding; FSW is their home ground. Copper, magnesium, steel and titanium are also welded this way.

Defects: a tunnel or wormhole when the tool travels too fast for metal to fill behind it; a kissing bond, an unbonded line where oxide was never broken; excess flash; tool wear. Chapter 4.9 covers inspection.
Uses: ship deck panels, train floor panels, rocket fuel tanks, battery trays and heat sinks.

Ultrasonic welding clamps parts between a vibrating tip (sonotrode) and an anvil and applies lateral shear vibration at 20 to 40 kHz. The vibration scrubs the surfaces, cracks the oxide film and lets clean metal bond under clamp force. Bulk temperature stays far below melting, so foils, dissimilar pairs such as aluminium to copper, IC wire bonds and plastics are welded this way.

Explosive welding stands a flyer plate at a small stand-off above a base plate and lays explosive on top. Detonation drives the flyer down at an angle. The collision point sweeps along and throws a jet of metal out of the closing gap; the jet strips oxide from both surfaces and very high pressure bonds them. The interface comes out wavy, the sign of a sound bond. Large clad plates — stainless steel on carbon steel, aluminium or titanium on steel — for chemical vessels and ship hulls are made this way.

Diffusion bonding holds cleaned parts in vacuum at 0.5 to 0.8 T<sub>m</sub> under a few MPa for minutes to hours. Atoms diffuse across the interface and the bond forms with almost no deformation; titanium, ceramics and honeycomb panels are joined so. Cold pressure welding and roll bonding use no external heat: heavy deformation breaks the oxide and extrudes fresh metal, and a rolling mill presses two strips into one bimetal sheet.

figure.caption: Friction stir welding from plunge to finished weld. The metal is only softened to about 0.8 of its melting point and stirred, never melted, so the stir zone is left as solid wrought metal.

spec.title: Friction stir welding cycle
spec.aria: A left-to-right chain of five blocks: the tool rotates, plunges into the plate, friction heats the metal to about 0.8 of the melting point, softened metal flows around the pin, and a stir zone with no melting is left behind.

examples.question: Two 25 mm diameter steel rods are joined by rotary friction welding. The chuck turns at 1500 rev/min, the axial friction pressure is 40 MPa and the coefficient of friction at the interface is 0.5. Find the rubbing speed at the interface and the friction power dissipated.
steps: Contact area: A = πD²/4 = π × 0.025² / 4 = 4.909 × 10⁻⁴ m².
Friction power: P = F_f × v = 9817 × 1.963 = 19 277 W ≈ 19.3 kW.
examples.answer: The rubbing speed is 1.96 m/s and the friction power is about 19.3 kW (19 277 W).
examples.check:
import math
D = 0.025
N = 1500.0
p = 40e6
mu = 0.5
v = math.pi * D * N / 60
A = math.pi * D * D / 4
F = p * A
Ff = mu * F
P = Ff * v
print(round(v, 2))
print(round(A, 6))
print(int(round(F)))
print(int(round(Ff)))
print(round(P / 1000, 2))

traps: Friction stir welding does not melt the metal. It softens it to about 0.8 of the melting point; no molten pool forms.
Friction welding is not limited to round bars. Linear friction welding oscillates one flat part against another and joins blisk blades and other non-round shapes.
Friction welding and friction stir welding are different. In friction welding one part spins; in FSW a separate tool spins and the parts stay still.
Explosive welding does not melt the plates. The jet cleans both surfaces and the bond is solid-state; any local melt is thrown out with the jet.
Ultrasonic welding is a joining process. Ultrasonic inspection is a different use of ultrasound and belongs with the defect methods of chapter 4.9.

quiz.q: Define solid-state welding in one sentence.
quiz.a: A joining process in which the parent metal never melts: clean surfaces are pressed into intimate contact and, with heat and time, atoms diffuse across the interface to form the bond.

quiz.q: Name the two features of a friction stir welding tool.
quiz.a: A shoulder — a flat disc that rubs the top surface — and a pin or probe, a short stub that projects into the joint line.

quiz.q: Why is a burn-off stage needed in friction welding?
quiz.a: It squeezes out softened metal carrying oxide and dirt from the original faces, so fresh metal meets fresh metal when the upset force is applied.

quiz.q: Why does friction stir welding suit 2xxx and 7xxx aluminium alloys better than arc welding?
quiz.a: Those alloys hot crack, porosify or lose strength when melted. FSW keeps the metal solid, so cast-nugget problems never arise and wrought structure survives.

quiz.q: A 20 mm diameter steel bar is friction welded at 1200 rev/min with a friction pressure of 30 MPa and μ = 0.4. Find the rubbing speed and the friction power.
A friction stir weld shows a tunnel on the advancing side. Suggest two process changes and say why each helps.
quiz.a: Reduce traverse speed or raise rotation speed. Both raise heat input and give softened metal time to fill the cavity behind the pin. Also check plunge depth so the shoulder forges the top surface.

quiz.q: Why does explosive welding give a wavy interface, and why is the wave treated as a good sign?
quiz.a: The jet at the collision point is unstable and oscillates as it sweeps along, rippling the interface. A regular wave shows collision angle and velocity were right; a flat interface means too little energy, and a melted interface means too much.

beyond: Not for the exam. Friction stir welding now runs in robotic and stationary-shoulder versions, and refill tools remove the exit hole. Additive friction stir deposition builds metal layers without melting the feedstock. Explosive cladding supplies bimetal plate for large pressure vessels and aluminium-to-steel transition joints. Diffusion bonding is the standard route to titanium honeycomb and ceramic-to-metal seals.
